text: So putting myself in the shoes of those particular companies, like I said, I think some of my most rewarding interactions have been with these non Silicon Valley companies.
speaker: John Cutler
context: Lenny asks John about the differences between Silicon Valley product teams and companies going through digital transformations. John explains that much of the advice available online is geared toward Silicon Valley startups, but most product managers work at companies that don't fit that mold. He shares that some of his most rewarding work has been with non-Silicon Valley companies that are trying to transform their approach to building products.
text_ko: 제가 그 회사들 입장이 돼서 생각해 보면, 말씀드렸듯이 가장 보람 있었던 만남 중 일부는 실리콘밸리 밖에 있는 회사들과의 교류였어요. 물론 베이 에어리어(Bay Area)나 미국에 있는 그런 회사들과 얘기할 때도 많은 걸 배워요.
text_zh: 所以站在那些公司的角度来看，就像我刚才说的，我觉得跟这些非硅谷公司打交道是最有收获的。当然了，跟湾区和美国其他地方的公司聊天，我也学到很多东西。
text_es: Entonces, poniéndome en el lugar de esas empresas en particular, como te decía, creo que algunas de mis interacciones más gratificantes han sido con estas empresas que no son del Silicon Valley. Definitivamente aprendo muchísimo cuando hablo con empresas de la Bahía de San Francisco y de Estados Unidos para hacer esas cosas específicas.
key_sentence: Rewarding interactions often come from non Silicon Valley companies.
original_text: So putting myself in the shoes of those particular companies, like I said, I think some of my most rewarding interactions have been with these non Silicon Valley companies. I certainly learn a lot when I talk to companies in the Bay Area and in the United States to do those particular things.

vocabulary.definition: Providing satisfaction or a sense of achievement; fulfilling.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a rewarding experience often refers to successful collaborations or projects that yield positive outcomes, both personally and professionally.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'rewarding' generally has a positive connotation, it can imply that the effort involved was significant, making the outcome particularly gratifying.

vocabulary.definition: The communication or direct involvement between individuals or groups.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, interactions can refer to exchanges between employees, clients, or stakeholders that can influence relationships and outcomes.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply both formal and informal exchanges; however, it often suggests a level of engagement that is more than just transactional.

vocabulary.definition: The integration of digital technology into all areas of a business, fundamentally changing how it operates and delivers value to customers.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the tech and startup sectors, digital transformations are crucial for enhancing efficiency, improving customer experiences, and staying competitive in a rapidly evolving market.
vocabulary.nuance: This term often carries the implication of significant change and investment, suggesting that it is not merely an upgrade but a complete overhaul of business processes.

vocabulary.definition: Designed or intended for a specific purpose or audience.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, products or services that are geared toward a particular demographic or market segment are tailored to meet the specific needs and preferences of that group.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase suggests a targeted approach, often implying that the offering is customized or optimized for the intended audience, rather than being generic.

text: Part of the thing is just realizing how much inertia they're up against when you're chatting them.
speaker: John Cutler
context: John continues discussing the challenges faced by larger enterprise companies trying to adopt modern product practices. He explains that these companies face significant organizational inertia - resistance to change built into their existing structures and processes. Some structural barriers can be overcome, while others are simply inherent to operating at that scale and in those industries.
text_ko: 일부는 그들과 얘기할 때 그들이 얼마나 큰 관성(inertia)에 맞서고 있는지를 깨닫는 것뿐이에요. 그래서 피할 수 있는 구조적 문제들(structural)이 분명히 있다고 생각해요. 하지만 어쩔 수 없이 그 과정의 일부로 존재하는 구조적 요소들도 있어요.
text_zh: 其实很大一部分原因就是，你跟他们聊的时候会发现，他们面临的阻力有多大。所以我觉得有些结构性的问题他们可能是能避免的，但还有一些结构性的问题就是游戏规则的一部分，没办法。
text_es: Parte del asunto es darse cuenta de cuánta inercia tienen en contra cuando estás hablando con ellos. Así que sí creo que hay algunas cosas estructurales que probablemente podrían evitar, pero también hay cosas estructurales que simplemente son parte del juego para hacer eso.
key_sentence: how much inertia they're up against
original_text: Part of the thing is just realizing how much inertia they're up against when you're chatting them. So I do believe that there's some structural things that probably they could avoid, but then there's also just structural things that are just part of the game to do that.

vocabulary.definition: Inertia refers to a tendency to remain unchanged or resist change, often due to established habits or systems.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, inertia can manifest as resistance to new ideas or innovations, making it challenging for organizations to adapt to market changes or implement new strategies.
vocabulary.nuance: While inertia can indicate stability, it often carries a negative connotation, suggesting stagnation or an unwillingness to evolve.

vocabulary.definition: Organizational pertains to the arrangement or structure of a company or institution, including its systems, processes, and culture.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, organizational structures dictate how roles, responsibilities, and communication flow within a company, impacting efficiency and effectiveness.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply a focus on systematic processes and hierarchy, which may be viewed positively in structured environments but negatively in more dynamic, flexible settings.

vocabulary.definition: To adopt means to take up, accept, or start to use something, such as a practice, policy, or idea.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, companies often adopt new technologies or practices to improve operations, enhance competitiveness, or respond to market demands.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'adopt' suggests a proactive choice, it can also imply a lack of originality, as it often refers to taking on existing ideas rather than creating new ones.

vocabulary.definition: Practices refer to established methods or procedures that are regularly followed in a particular field or profession.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business realm, best practices are often identified as effective strategies that lead to optimal outcomes, guiding companies in their operations and decision-making.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply a level of standardization and routine, which may be beneficial for consistency but can also lead to rigidity if not periodically reassessed.

text: So I think that for a lot of those companies, they see adopting the frameworks as the end goal. They kind of look there.
speaker: John Cutler
context: John discusses a common mistake that transforming companies make when trying to adopt modern product practices. Instead of understanding the principles behind successful product development, these companies focus on copying the specific frameworks and tools used by successful companies like Figma. John argues this approach misses the point - frameworks should be learning tools, not end goals in themselves.
text_ko: 저는 많은 회사들이 프레임워크(frameworks)를 도입하는 걸 그 자체 목표로 보는 것 같아요. 그래서 거기에만 초점을 맞추는 편이고요. 가끔 글을 써서 'Figma가 어떻게 작동하나요?'라고 물어봐도, '우린 이런 프레임워크만 써요'라고만 답하더라고요.
text_zh: 所以我觉得很多公司都把采用这些框架当成最终目标了。他们就盯着这个看。有时候你可能写个帖子问"Figma是怎么运作的？"他们就回答说"我们用这些框架。"
text_es: Entonces creo que muchas de esas empresas ven adoptar los marcos de trabajo (frameworks) como el objetivo final. Como que se enfocan en eso. Y a veces hasta escribes un post preguntando "¿Cómo funciona Figma?" y te responden "Nosotros usamos estos frameworks."
key_sentence: They see adopting frameworks as the end goal.
original_text: So I think that for a lot of those companies, they see adopting the frameworks as the end goal. They kind of look there. And sometimes maybe even you write a post, it's like, 'Well, how does Figma work?' And they're like, 'We use these frameworks.'

vocabulary.definition: The act of accepting or starting to use something new, such as a method, idea, or technology.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, adopting often refers to the integration of new practices or technologies that can enhance efficiency and competitiveness.
vocabulary.nuance: While adopting implies a positive acceptance, it can also suggest a lack of critical evaluation of the new practice or technology.

vocabulary.definition: Structured systems or guidelines that provide a foundation for understanding and organizing complex concepts or processes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, frameworks are often used to standardize processes, facilitate project management, and ensure consistency across teams.
vocabulary.nuance: Frameworks can imply a level of flexibility within a structured approach, but may also suggest rigidity if too strictly enforced.

vocabulary.definition: Fundamental truths or propositions that serve as the foundation for a system of belief or behavior.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, principles guide decision-making, corporate culture, and ethical standards, influencing how organizations operate.
vocabulary.nuance: Principles often carry a moral weight, suggesting that they are not just guidelines but also reflect core values of an organization.

vocabulary.definition: The process of bringing a new product to market, encompassing the entire lifecycle from ideation to design, production, and launch.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups and tech companies, product development is crucial for innovation and competitive advantage, often involving iterative testing and user feedback.
vocabulary.nuance: Product development can imply a collaborative and dynamic process, but may also suggest a risk of failure if not managed effectively.

text: And so I think that the way that I tend to think about frameworks is that they're more like a job aid. They're more like a learning tool that the team kind of uses to keep themself on track.
speaker: John Cutler
context: John explains his philosophy on how frameworks should be used in product development. Rather than treating frameworks as rigid processes that must be followed exactly, he views them as job aids - tools that help teams learn and stay focused. Successful companies adapt and modify frameworks when they're not working, rather than blindly following them regardless of results.
text_ko: 그래서 저는 프레임워크(frameworks)를 오히려 업무 보조 도구(job aid)처럼 보는 편이에요. 팀이 스스로 길을 잃지 않게 도와주는 학습 도구 같은 거고요. 다만 잘 안 풀리면 그런 회사들은 쓰고 있던 것들을 다시 만들어 버리기도 해요.
text_zh: 所以我觉得吧，框架(framework)这个东西更像是一个工作辅助工具。就是团队用来让自己不跑偏的学习工具。但关键是，如果现有的东西不好用了，那些公司会重新发明他们在用的工具。
text_es: Y entonces, yo creo que la forma en que suelo ver los frameworks es más como una herramienta de apoyo en el trabajo. Son más como una herramienta de aprendizaje que el equipo usa para mantenerse enfocado. Pero lo que pasa es que esas empresas van a reinventar las cosas que están usando cuando no les están funcionando.
key_sentence: Frameworks serve as a job aid to keep themself on track.
original_text: And so I think that the way that I tend to think about frameworks is that they're more like a job aid. They're more like a learning tool that the team kind of uses to keep themself on track. But part of the thing is that those companies will reinvent the things they're using when things aren't working out.

vocabulary.definition: Frameworks are structured systems or guidelines that provide a foundation for understanding or developing concepts, processes, or projects.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, frameworks are often used to standardize practices, facilitate collaboration, and ensure consistency across teams and projects.
vocabulary.nuance: Frameworks imply a level of flexibility and adaptability, allowing teams to customize their approach while adhering to established principles.

vocabulary.definition: A job aid is a tool or resource designed to assist employees in performing specific tasks or processes more efficiently and effectively.
vocabulary.businessContext: In corporate settings, job aids can take various forms, such as checklists, flowcharts, or instructional guides, and are used to enhance productivity and reduce errors.
vocabulary.nuance: Job aids are typically practical and straightforward, focusing on immediate task performance rather than broader learning objectives.

vocabulary.definition: A learning tool is any resource or technology that facilitates the acquisition of knowledge or skills, often through interactive or engaging methods.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the corporate environment, learning tools can include e-learning platforms, simulations, or workshops that support employee development and training initiatives.
vocabulary.nuance: Learning tools are often associated with a more formal educational context, emphasizing the process of learning rather than just task completion.

vocabulary.definition: On track refers to being in alignment with established goals, timelines, or plans, indicating progress toward a desired outcome.
vocabulary.businessContext: In project management and team dynamics, being on track is crucial for ensuring that deliverables are met within deadlines and that objectives are achieved.
vocabulary.nuance: The phrase carries a positive connotation, suggesting that progress is being made as intended, and can be contrasted with being 'off track' or behind schedule.

text: And I talk about this a lot, this sort of I do believe there's sort of this fundamental attribution bias at play where people in these high performings don't acknowledge the amount that luck and inertia has been a part of what they're doing.
speaker: John Cutler
context: Lenny and John are discussing why advice from successful Silicon Valley companies doesn't always work for other organizations. John explains that there's a cognitive bias where successful companies and leaders attribute their success primarily to their skills and decisions, while underestimating the role of luck, timing, and favorable circumstances. This leads to advice that may not be applicable to companies in different situations.
text_ko: 저는 이 얘기를 자주 하는데, 일종의 근본적 귀인 편향(fundamental attribution bias)이 있어서 성과가 높은 사람들일수록 자신들이 해온 일에 운과 관성이 얼마나 기여했는지를 잘 인정하지 않는다고 생각해요.
text_zh: 我经常说这个问题，我觉得这里面有个根本归因偏误(fundamental attribution bias)在起作用，就是那些业绩特别好的人，他们不愿意承认运气和惯性在他们成功中占了多大分量。
text_es: Y hablo mucho de esto, creo que hay como un sesgo de atribución fundamental (fundamental attribution bias) en juego donde la gente que tiene mucho éxito no reconoce hasta qué punto la suerte y la inercia han sido parte de lo que han logrado.
key_sentence: Fundamental attribution bias at play affects high performings' perceptions.

vocabulary.definition: Essential or foundational; serving as a basis for something.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'fundamental' often refers to core principles or elements that underpin strategies, models, or operations.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'fundamental' implies something crucial, it can sometimes suggest a lack of flexibility or adaptability in approach.

vocabulary.definition: A cognitive bias that affects how individuals interpret and assign causes to events, often leading to skewed perceptions of responsibility or success.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the workplace, attribution bias can influence performance evaluations, team dynamics, and leadership decisions by attributing success or failure to individual effort rather than external factors.
vocabulary.nuance: Attribution bias can lead to misunderstandings and unfair assessments, making it important to consider external influences when evaluating outcomes.

vocabulary.definition: Exhibiting superior performance or productivity, often exceeding standard expectations.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a corporate setting, 'high performing' teams or individuals are recognized for their exceptional results and contributions to organizational goals.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'high performing' conveys excellence, it can also imply pressure and expectations that may lead to burnout if not managed properly.

vocabulary.definition: A tendency to remain unchanged or resist movement, often due to established habits or systems.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, inertia can refer to the reluctance to change processes, strategies, or organizational structures, which can hinder innovation and adaptation.
vocabulary.nuance: While inertia can provide stability, it can also stifle growth and responsiveness in a rapidly changing market environment.

text: And that the people in the big companies, or these not, these companies that believe that it's not the way that they can do that actually overestimate the kind of systemic drag in their organization and underestimate what can be possible.
speaker: John Cutler
context: John continues explaining the attribution bias that affects how companies view their ability to change. While successful companies underestimate the role of luck in their success, struggling companies tend to overestimate the barriers holding them back (systemic drag) and underestimate what improvements are actually possible within their constraints.
text_ko: 대기업에 있는 사람들이나 '그건 우리가 못 해'라고 믿는 회사들은 조직의 시스템적 저항(systemic drag)을 과대평가하고 실제로 가능한 것들은 과소평가해요.
text_zh: 那些大公司的人，或者说那些认为这样做不可行的公司，其实都高估了自己组织内部的体系阻力(systemic drag)，低估了真正能做到的事情。
text_es: Y la gente de las empresas grandes, o bueno, estas empresas que creen que no es la forma en que pueden hacerlo, en realidad sobreestiman la inercia del sistema (systemic drag) que tienen en su organización y subestiman lo que realmente se puede lograr.
key_sentence: They overestimate systemic drag and underestimate what can be possible.

vocabulary.definition: Systemic drag refers to the inherent inefficiencies or obstacles within an organization that slow down progress or hinder performance.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, systemic drag can manifest as bureaucratic processes, outdated technologies, or cultural resistance to change, impacting a company's ability to innovate and respond to market demands.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often carries a negative connotation, suggesting that these inefficiencies are deeply embedded and difficult to eliminate.

vocabulary.definition: To overestimate means to assess or judge something as being greater or more significant than it actually is.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business contexts, overestimating can lead to unrealistic projections in sales forecasts, resource allocation, or project timelines, potentially resulting in strategic missteps.
vocabulary.nuance: While overestimating can stem from optimism, it may also indicate a lack of data or understanding, and should be approached with caution in decision-making.

vocabulary.definition: To underestimate means to assess or judge something as being less significant or less capable than it actually is.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, underestimating can lead to missed opportunities, such as undervaluing a competitor's capabilities or the potential of a new market.
vocabulary.nuance: Underestimating often reflects a lack of thorough analysis or awareness, and can result in strategic errors if not recognized.

vocabulary.definition: Attribution bias refers to the systematic errors made when people evaluate or try to find reasons for their own or others' behaviors, often attributing success to internal factors and failures to external ones.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, attribution bias can affect performance evaluations, team dynamics, and leadership decisions, leading to skewed perceptions of employee contributions and accountability.
vocabulary.nuance: This bias can hinder objective analysis and decision-making, making it essential for leaders to be aware of their own biases when assessing performance.

text: I think that what I realized over the course of these four years is that I wanted to pivot back to help put most of my energy into helping my own company.
speaker: John Cutler
context: John explains why he's leaving his role as Product Evangelist at Amplitude to join Toast. After four years of helping hundreds of different companies improve their product practices, he wants to focus his energy on helping one company - Toast - which is experiencing rapid growth and has multiple business lines beyond just their core point-of-sale business.
text_ko: 이 4년 동안 깨달은 건 제가 다시 제 회사 쪽으로 방향을 틀어(pivot back) 제 에너지 대부분을 그쪽에 쏟고 싶었다는 거예요. 회사가 엄청 빨리 커지고 있어서 거의 모든 수치가 수백 단위거나 많게는 수천 단위예요.
text_zh: 我觉得这四年下来我意识到，我想要转回去(pivot)，把大部分精力都投入到帮助自己的公司上。他们现在发展特别快，各项数据都是几百几千这个量级的。
text_es: Creo que lo que me di cuenta durante estos cuatro años es que quería cambiar de rumbo y enfocar la mayor parte de mi energía en ayudar a mi propia empresa. Están creciendo súper rápido, así que las cifras están en cientos de todo o en miles de todo.
key_sentence: I wanted to pivot back to help my company grow super fast.
original_text: I think that what I realized over the course of these four years is that I wanted to pivot back to help put most of my energy into helping my own company. They're growing super fast, so the numbers are in the hundreds of everything or in the thousands of everything.

vocabulary.definition: To change direction or strategy, often in response to new information or circumstances.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, particularly in startups, 'pivoting' refers to a significant shift in a company's business model or product strategy to better meet market demands or improve performance.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'pivot' suggests a strategic and often positive change, it can also imply that the previous approach was unsuccessful.

vocabulary.definition: The capacity to do work or produce change; in a business context, it often refers to the enthusiasm and effort put into tasks.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the corporate environment, 'energy' can describe the motivation and vigor employees bring to their roles, which can significantly impact productivity and innovation.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'energy' generally has a positive connotation, it can also imply a sense of urgency or pressure when discussing workloads.

vocabulary.definition: The concentration of attention or effort on a particular task or objective.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, maintaining 'focus' is crucial for achieving strategic goals and ensuring that resources are effectively allocated to priority areas.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'focus' is often associated with productivity and clarity, it can also suggest a narrowing of perspective that may overlook other important factors.

vocabulary.definition: To make or become better in quality, value, or performance.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, 'improvement' is often linked to processes, products, or services, indicating a commitment to enhancing efficiency and customer satisfaction.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'improve' implies a positive change, but it can also suggest that the current state is inadequate or requires enhancement.
